newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to hail drop in federal budget deficit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to hail drop in federal budget deficit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton plans to announce on Monday figures showing that the federal budget deficit has fallen to its lowest level in 15 years.
White House officials said Clinton was expected to unveil the budget deficit for fiscal 1996, which ended Sept. 30, at a St. Louis campaign rally.
They declined to disclose the deficit figure itself, but it has been widely discussed over the past few weeks by administration and congressional officials, who put it at roughly $109 billion.

Earlier this month, the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated in a confidential memo that the deficit was between $107 billion and $111 billion, well below 1995's $163.9 billion shortfall.
In May it estimated the deficit at $144 billion and at $116 billion in August, in part because of higher tax revenues from stronger-than-expected economic growth.
If the actual number, compiled by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), comes in at around $109 billion, it would be the lowest since 1981, when the deficit stood at $79 billiion.
"There will be some news related to the budget deficit ... that will be very encouraging," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters on Sunday, declining to give figures.
White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta also hinted on a Sunday television interview programme that Clinton would have "some good news" to announce on the deficit.

Clinton's use of the OMB figures with only eight days until his Nov. 5 showdown against Republican Bob Dole, whom he leads by double digits according to national opinion polls, was a textbook example of the powers of incumbency.

Knowing that the confidential figures were to be released, Clinton was able to build a campaign speech around them and to fly out some of his economic officials, including OMB Director Franklin Raines, to brief the media.
Seeking to steal Clinton's thunder, Republicans on Sunday said that the deficit would be around $109 billion and sought to prevent Clinton from taking credit.

"This accomplishment comes as good news to every American but a complete surprise to Bill Clinton, who should get absolutely no credit for it," House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich, an Ohio Republican, said in a statement.
The budget, and efforts to bring it under control, have been the focus of some of the roughest U.S. political battles of the past year, leading to two shutdowns of the federal government.
Clinton has repeatedly boasted in campaign appearances that the federal budget has fallen in each of the four years of his presidency, a feat last accomplished before the Civil War.
He has also argued that his efforts to reduce the deficit have helped keep interest rates down, spurring economic growth.

"Your votes will decide whether we balance the budget and move away from the dangerous and reckless fiscal policies that quadrupled our debt in the 12 years before I came to Washington ...," Clinton told a rally in Springfield, Virginia on Sunday.

"Whether we balance the budget in a way that ... still protects the fundamentals of educational investment, research investment, protection of the environment (and) Medicaid's guarantee of health care to people with disabilities," he added.
Clinton was scheduled make speeches in Minneapolis, and Chicago on Monday and in Columbus, Ohio and Chicago on Tuesday, before returning to the White House for a one-night stopover.
On Wednesday, he leaves for his final, seven-day campaign blitz that will culminate in Little Rock, Arkansas, where he will spend election night.
